claims.text: Citizen Kane (1941) follows a reporter trying to learn what Charles Foster Kane meant by his last word, 'Rosebud'.
The Maltese Falcon, The Lady from Shanghai and Sunset Boulevard are not built around a search for the meaning of Rosebud.
Orson Welles was 25 when he co-wrote, directed, produced and starred in Citizen Kane.
Gregg Toland's deep-focus cinematography on Citizen Kane kept near and distant objects sharp in the same shot.

writerNotes: Self-check 9.3. Lint: clean. Claims: every claim listed, risk at or above the C26 floor; the schema's riskReason list has no only or counterintuitive, so such claims carry the nearest listed reason. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers film or TV facts, so every high-risk claim here needs checker evidence from the web. Rival test: The Maltese Falcon is also from 1941 and The Lady from Shanghai is another Welles film, but neither involves Rosebud. Sunset Boulevard (1950) is narrated by a dead writer, a different hook. Volatility: evergreen; no time words; nothing depends on events after mid-2026. Regional: the work is known worldwide and the options need no single country's local knowledge. Style: Oxford spelling, straight single quotes, plain hyphens, explanation of 27 words. Myths: claims screened against myths.json, no match. Mystery and encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: Welles was 25 while shooting in 1940 and turned 26 days after the May 1941 release, so c3 says 25 when he made it.

evidence.restatement: The other three films have different plots (a hunt for a jewelled statuette, a noir about a sailor and a femme fatale, a faded silent star's mansion); none turns on Rosebud.

Welles, born 6 May 1915, shot Citizen Kane between June and October 1940 and saw it premiere on 1 May 1941, so he was 25 throughout; he co-wrote it with Herman J. Mankiewicz, and directed, produced and starred in it.
